passages.happening:
“One day Samson went to Gaza, where he saw a prostitute and went in to spend the night with her” (verse 1).

The men of Gaza hear that he is there. They surround the place and lie in wait at the city gate all night, planning to kill him at dawn (verse 2).

But Samson gets up at midnight. He takes hold of the doors of the city gate and both gateposts, pulls them up, bar and all, puts them on his shoulders, and carries them to the top of the hill that faces Hebron (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
Gaza was the southernmost of the five Philistine cities, near the coast. Samson walks into the heart of the enemy's country for a night with a prostitute. The appetites that ruled him at Timnah are still ruling him.

The city gate was a town's defense and its pride. Its doors were barred at night. Samson carries off the whole thing, doors, posts and bar.

Hebron lay in the hills of Judah, about forty miles east of Gaza and some three thousand feet higher. Whether Samson carried the gates all that way, or to a hill on the way that looks toward Hebron, is debated. Either way, the feat is enormous, and the shame for Gaza is great.

The chapter begins the way the end of Samson's story will go: a woman, enemies lying in wait, and his great strength. This time the strength carries him out. The next time it will not.
passages.later:
The book of Joshua lists Gaza among the cities left in the hands of the Philistines: “the five Philistine rulers of Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron” (Joshua 13:3).

The wisdom books warn about the road Samson keeps walking: “Do not lust in your heart for her beauty or let her captivate you with her eyes” (Proverbs 6:25).
passages.asks: Samson walked into an enemy city for the sake of a night's pleasure, and his strength got him out. Ask where you have come to count on getting away with something because you always have before. And ask what you would do differently if you knew this was the last time.

passages.happening:
Some time later Samson falls in love with a woman in the valley of Sorek named Delilah (verse 4). The lords of the Philistines come to her. “Entice him and find out the source of his great strength and how we can overpower him to tie him up and subdue him. Then each one of us will give you eleven hundred shekels of silver” (verse 5).

Three times she asks him. Three times he gives a false answer: seven fresh bowstrings, new ropes, his seven braids woven into a loom. Three times she binds him, cries, “Samson, the Philistines are here!” and he breaks free (verses 6-14).

“How can you say, ‘I love you,’” she asked, “when your heart is not with me?” (verse 15). She presses him day after day until he is sick to death of it (verse 16). Then he tells her everything. “My hair has never been cut, because I have been a Nazirite to God from my mother’s womb. If I am shaved, my strength will leave me, and I will become as weak as any other man” (verse 17).

She sends for the lords, and they come with the money (verse 18). She lulls him to sleep on her lap and calls a man to shave off the seven braids, and his strength leaves him (verse 19). “Samson, the Philistines are here!” He wakes and thinks he will shake himself free as before. “But he did not know that the LORD had departed from him” (verse 20).

The Philistines seize him, gouge out his eyes, take him down to Gaza, bind him in bronze shackles, and set him to grind grain in the prison (verse 21). “However, the hair of his head began to grow back after it had been shaved” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
The valley of Sorek is the same valley that runs past Samson's home and Timnah. The text does not say whether Delilah was a Philistine or an Israelite.

The bribe was enormous. Five lords each promised eleven hundred shekels of silver, about five thousand five hundred in all. In the next chapter a priest is hired for ten shekels a year.

The story is built on a pattern of three and then a fourth. Each false answer comes a little closer to the truth: the third already involves his hair. A reader wonders why Samson keeps sleeping in her house after each betrayal. The story does not explain him. It shows a man whose desires had stopped listening to anything else. The verb the lords use, entice, is the one the men of Timnah used to his wife, and the two betrayals mirror each other.

Then the saddest sentence in his story: ‘he did not know that the LORD had departed from him’. His strength was never really in his hair. It was the LORD's. The hair was the last outward sign of his being set apart to God, a vow he had long neglected. When the last sign went, the LORD's strength went with it, and Samson did not notice. The same Hebrew verb is used for his strength leaving and for the LORD departing.

Blinding prisoners and making them grind grain were known practices in that world. Grinding was hard, lowly work usually given to women and slaves. For a war hero it was meant as public shame.

Verse 22 is a quiet note of hope. His hair begins to grow back.
passages.later:
The proverbs describe the slow way a person is caught: “He follows her on impulse, like an ox going to the slaughter” (Proverbs 7:22).

A psalm prays the prayer Samson never prayed until it was almost too late: “Cast me not away from Your presence; take not Your Holy Spirit from me” (Psalm 51:11).
passages.asks: Samson did not know that the LORD had left him. Ask whether you could be drifting from God so slowly that you would not notice what you had lost. And ask where you are being pressed day after day by something that is wearing you down, and who could stand with you before you give in.

passages.happening:
The lords of the Philistines gather to offer a great sacrifice to their god Dagon and to celebrate. “Our god has delivered Samson our enemy into our hands” (verse 23). The people praise their god when they see him (verse 24).

In high spirits they call Samson out of prison to entertain them, and they stand him between the pillars (verse 25). He asks the servant who leads him by the hand to let him feel the pillars that hold up the temple so that he can lean on them (verse 26). The temple is full of men and women, all the lords of the Philistines are there, and about three thousand more are on the roof watching him (verse 27).

Then Samson calls out to the LORD: “O Lord GOD, please remember me. Strengthen me, O God, just once more, so that with one vengeful blow I may pay back the Philistines for my two eyes” (verse 28).

He takes hold of the two central pillars, one with each hand (verse 29). He says, “Let me die with the Philistines.” Then he pushes with all his might, and the temple falls on the lords and all the people in it. “So in his death he killed more than he had killed in his life” (verse 30).

His brothers and his father's family come down, carry him home, and bury him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of his father Manoah. He had judged Israel twenty years (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
In the ancient world a victory was credited to the god of the winning people. So the Philistines praise Dagon. The story becomes a contest, not between Samson and the Philistines, but between the LORD and Dagon.

Dagon was an old god of the Semitic world, worshiped in Syria and Mesopotamia long before the Philistines came, and they adopted him. The older idea that he was a fish-god is now generally doubted. His name is related to a word for grain, and many scholars think he was a god of grain or of storms.

Excavations at Tell Qasile, a Philistine site near Tel Aviv, have uncovered a temple from this period whose roof rested on two central wooden pillars set on stone bases. It helps a reader picture the scene.

Samson's last prayer begins well, ‘please remember me’. In the Old Testament, when God remembers someone, as he remembered Noah and Hannah, he acts for them. But the prayer ends with revenge for his two eyes. Even here his motive is mixed.

God answers him. The temple falls on the lords and the crowd. The judge who was to begin Israel's deliverance ends as a blind prisoner whose death strikes a heavy blow against Israel's oppressors.

After this, the book has no more deliverers. Samson is the last judge whose story it tells.
passages.later:
The contest between the LORD and Dagon continues in the next book, when the Philistines set the captured ark beside Dagon's statue: “there was Dagon, fallen on his face before the ark of the LORD” (1 Samuel 5:3).

The letter to the Hebrews names Samson among those who acted by faith (Hebrews 11:32). The site's notes on that chapter say why such people are there: God works through flawed people who trust him, and naming them is not approval of every act they did.
passages.hard:
Was Samson's last act a suicide? And how could God answer a prayer for revenge?

The question has been debated for centuries. Some readers, among them Augustine in The City of God, argued that Samson's death was not a sinful suicide, because he acted by a special prompting of God, shown by God's answer to his prayer. Others see his act as a warrior's death in battle, taking his enemies with him, and not a suicide in the modern sense. Still others think his motive was mixed at best, since he asked to pay the Philistines back for his two eyes, and that God answered him because of his larger purpose for Israel, not because the motive was pure.

The narrator gives no verdict on Samson's heart. The answered prayer shows that God had not finished with him. The chapter shows Samson's failure, God's patience, and God's victory over Dagon. It gives no one a pattern to follow.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Samson's hair grew back, and his last prayer was heard. Ask what his story says about grace after failure, and whether you believe there is any for you. And notice that he asked God to remember him. Ask what you would say if you prayed that prayer today.
